title: Skip the Compressor:Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files

paper.title: Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files
paper.abstract:
Abstract A coding agent works on repositories that can be far larger than its context window can hold.
Prompt compressors and retrievers offer solutions to this problem, but patching an issue needs two things at once: the files that must change, and their code exactly as written, since the model must reproduce the lines it edits.
Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget.
We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks.
We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark’s tests.
With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers.
CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3).
Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) now resolve real software issues end to end: they read an issue, explore a repository and write a patch that the project’s tests accept ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2025 ) . Managing what enters their context already makes them cheaper: it can halve an agent’s cost ( Lindenbauer et al., 2025 ) or cut it by a fifth to a third ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) . Every prompt token is paid for on every call, and models use information in the middle of a long input less reliably than at its ends ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Figure 1: An issue sample under different compression methods. The issue ( pypa__twine-1225 ) reports error messages that lack the f of an f-string; the gold patch edits twine/sdist.py . ρ \rho : gold-file recall, the share of the gold-patch files in the context m m ; ε \varepsilon : the share of m m ’s lines that are verbatim. BM25 fills B i B_{i} with issue templates (two of three spans shown), so its patch guesses lines it never saw; LLMLingua-2 deletes tokens (struck out), among them the f of line 23, so its patch rewrites a line that does not exist; ours shows the file verbatim. Indentation is trimmed; an ellipsis marks an elided prefix. Chosen for illustration as the smallest of the 4 such issues out of 300 (a random one is in Appendix A ). Right: resolution with GPT-5.6 (solid) and Claude Opus 5 (light), every context fitted to B i B_{i} . SWE-Pruner, a line pruner trained for coding agents, is the last bar of the pruning group, and SweRank, a trained retriever of whole functions, the last bar of the retrieval group. Yet every step still needs code in the prompt, and a coding agent’s context window is small next to the repositories it works on: SWE-bench codebases average 3,010 non-test files and 438K lines ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) . We therefore treat the repository as the agent’s memory and the prompt as a compressed view of it, one that leaves most of the code out. To resolve an issue, the view still has to keep two things: the files the fix must edit, and their text exactly as it is. For anyone building a coding agent, this raises a practical question: at a fixed token budget, which compression of the repository lets the model resolve the most issues? Three lines of work each study part of this question: prompt compression for long natural-language prompts ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) , retrieval of repository code for code completion and issue resolution ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , and issue-resolution systems that prune what an agent reads ( Wang et al., 2026 ) or compress the context around known fault locations ( Jia et al., 2026 ) . Figure 1 shows how the first two can fail on one issue from our study, a report that some error messages lack the f of an f-string. A chunk retriever fills the budget with the repository’s issue templates, which share the report’s wording, and never shows the file to edit. A token pruner keeps that file but deletes f prefixes and quotation marks, so the model’s patch rewrites a line that does not exist and fails to apply. Shown the file whole and verbatim, the same model writes the fix. None of these lines of work compares retrieval, token pruning and file selection at a matched budget per issue, with each method free to decide which files enter the context. Both failures follow from how these tools work. Retrievers rank chunks or files by their similarity to the issue ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ; Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Suresh et al., 2025 ) , so text that echoes the report can outrank the file to edit. Prompt compressors delete the tokens or code blocks that a small model scores as least useful ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) ; this costs little when the output is an answer or a summary, but an edit must quote the code it changes exactly ( Xia et al., 2025 ; Anthropic, 2024 ; Gauthier, 2026 ) . The remedy follows: spend the budget on choosing which files to show, and show them whole and verbatim, so that edits quote text that exists and no compression model runs in the loop. Since each chosen file is shown whole, the selector must name few files, and the right ones. We therefore build a simple selector, CQ2-CARE, that asks the model under test twice, independently, which files must change and keeps the files both answers name, taking agreement between samples as a sign of reliability ( Wang et al., 2023 ) ; it then adds the short spans that grep finds for definitions, callers or strings the model requests, so code the fix depends on is shown verbatim even outside the chosen files. Its strength is its choice of unit, not its sampling scheme: a single answer cut to the same number of files does about as well, so what matters is choosing few files well (§ 4.4 ). We test this remedy in a controlled comparison on 300 issues from the SWE-rebench leaderboard ( Badertdinov et al., 2025 ) , one per repository: a fixed model receives the issue and one context fitted to the size of the CQ2-CARE context for that issue, writes one patch, and the benchmark’s harness grades it with the issue’s tests. We describe each context by its gold-file recall, the share of the files to edit that it contains, and by the share of its lines that are verbatim, and we run controlled tests that change one of the two at a time. With each of two model families, the selector resolves more issues than each of three compressors and three retrievers, among them SWE-bench’s file-level BM25; with Claude, its lead over one compressor, LLMLingua-2, is narrow. The losses separate cleanly: retrievers keep the text verbatim but often miss the files to edit, and token pruners keep those files but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Controlled tests show that each loss costs on its own: deleting tokens from the selector’s own contexts, with the files unchanged, costs about as much as the compressors lose in the main comparison, while a compressor that keeps whole lines matches the selector when it starts from the same files. The selector even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution: SWE-Pruner, a line pruner, and SweRank, a retriever that shows whole functions verbatim and comes within two points. Our contributions are as follows: • CQ2-CARE, a simple selector that spends the context budget on the files the model names and shows them verbatim, with no compression model (§ 2 ). • A budget-matched, test-graded comparison of CQ2-CARE with three prompt compressors, three retrievers, among them SWE-bench’s file-level BM25, and two methods trained for issue resolution, on 300 issues and two model families (§ 3.3 ). • A decomposition of the losses into gold-file recall and verbatim lines, with controlled tests that change one at a time (§ 4.1 – 4.2 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Data
sections.text: We use the SWE-rebench leaderboard ( Badertdinov et al., 2025 ) , which collects recent issues automatically, at a pinned revision with 860 Python tasks from 413 repositories; on the older SWE-bench Verified, models can often name the files to edit from the issue text alone, which its authors attribute in part to possible memorization ( Liang et al., 2026 ) . A salted hash drew 340 candidate issues, one per repository, before any model call. Each candidate passed an eligibility check in our harness: the gold patch resolves it and an empty patch does not (328 of 340 passed). The first 300 eligible issues form the population, created between January 2025 and May 2026; a hash-chosen subset of 100 is used for the rate sweep and the edit-format control.

sections.heading: 3.2 Setup and Baselines
sections.text: All methods share one pipeline and differ only in the context step (Appendix B ). CQ2-CARE (§ 2 ) draws five ranked answers per issue, of which a salted hash picks L 1 L_{1} , L 2 L_{2} and L 0 L_{0} ; with GPT-5.6, its context holds 1.7 selected files on average (median 1) and spans from 6.0 more files (variants in § 4.4 ). Figure 2: Why compressed contexts fail. (a) Gold-file recall ρ \rho and verbatim lines ε \varepsilon of every context, labelled with its resolution (GPT-5.6, 300 issues, budgets matched per issue; the gold files resolve 49.3%). Hollow markers: the two trained methods, SWE-Pruner and SweRank. (b) Gap to ours, the paired difference in resolution (row minus ours, points), on all 300 issues: a second patch sample; our contexts with 20% of every line’s tokens deleted; the main-study compressors, which cut the larger single-draw context; and, as a control rather than a baseline, the same compressors cutting our own candidate files to B i B_{i} . Bars: 95% issue-bootstrap intervals. The baselines are context steps an agent builder can drop in without training. Each compressor cuts m ~ \tilde{m} , the uncompressed context that the same pipeline builds from L 0 L_{0} alone, to B i B_{i} and keeps span headers verbatim ( m ~ \tilde{m} already fits in 52 issues and is used as is). We run the official implementations with their documented settings: LLMLingua-2 ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , LongLLMLingua ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Qwen Team et al., 2025 ) as the scorer, and LongCodeZip ( Shi et al., 2025 ) with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct ( Hui et al., 2024 ) . Chunk BM25 ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ) and dense retrieval with CodeRankEmbed ( Suresh et al., 2025 ) rank top-level Python definitions or 60-line windows against the issue and pack them in rank order up to B i B_{i} . File-level BM25, SWE-bench’s own retrieval baseline ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , adds whole non-test Python files in rank order while they fit, so it lands under B i B_{i} . Two methods trained for issue resolution were added after the main results, with the same prompt and grader and without tests, gold patches or fault locations (Algorithms 6 and 9 ): SWE-Pruner ( Wang et al., 2026 ) deletes lines from the single-draw context that the compressors cut at a threshold that fits B i B_{i} , and SweRank ( Reddy et al., 2026 ) ranks every non-test Python function against the issue; we show whole functions in that order up to B i B_{i} . For scale, the gold-file oracle (upper bound) shows the source files the gold patch modifies, and the no-source context shows the issue alone. The main table reports one model per family, each used for every call: gpt-5.6-sol (medium reasoning effort) and Claude Opus 5, both on all 300 issues. The model returns a unified diff from a prompt that differs across contexts only in the localized paths and the context, and we grade it with the SWE-rebench fork of the official harness ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Badertdinov et al., 2025 ) ; patches that fail to parse or apply count as unresolved (exit codes alone are not enough; Appendix C ). Comparisons are paired by issue: one-sided exact McNemar tests ( McNemar, 1947 ; Dror et al., 2018 ) , Holm-corrected ( Holm, 1979 ) within the compressors, with SWE-Pruner, and within the planned retrievers, with SweRank (Appendix Table 5 ), with 95% issue-bootstrap intervals ( Efron and Tibshirani, 1994 ) . The main tests follow a written plan, which we did not time-stamp; file-level BM25 and the analyses of § 4 are post hoc (Appendix D ).

sections.heading: 3.3 Main Results
sections.text: Exact files beat every drop-in baseline with both models (Table 1 ). CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% of the issues with GPT-5.6 and 46.7% with Claude Opus 5, 6.3 points more than the best compressor with either model and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best retriever. All these leads are significant, the narrowest (LLMLingua-2 with Claude, p = 0.027 p=0.027 ) only weakly. Whole files alone are not enough: SWE-bench’s file-level BM25 shows whole files chosen by similarity to the issue and trails by 9.3 and 12.7 points. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than the two trained methods: SWE-Pruner trails with both models, significantly only with Claude, and SweRank is within two points (§ 4.1 ). Exact files chosen by the model come close to the true ones: the gold files resolve 5.7 points more than CQ2-CARE with GPT-5.6 and no more with Claude. At the budget a compressor would use, an agent that chooses a few whole files recovers most of what knowing the files to edit would give it.

Chosen for illustration from the 12 issues where ours resolves and both chunk retrievers fail without showing any file to edit. Retrievers lose the files to edit (Figure 2 a). Ranking code by its similarity to the issue fills the budget with other code, tests and documentation (Table 2 ): chunk BM25 and dense retrieval put a fifth or less of their lines in the files to edit, against half for CQ2-CARE, and show none of them on over a quarter of the issues. On an issue that reports a shell script (Table 3 ), chunk BM25 fills the budget with tests that share its commands and dense retrieval with tests of the diff command, while the file to edit appears in neither. File-level BM25 shows whole files, so its patches apply more often and it resolves more than chunk BM25, but most of its lines still come from files the fix does not touch. SweRank, trained to rank functions for an issue, comes closest, 0.7 and 1.7 points behind, by showing whole functions verbatim, so its patches apply (97.3% and 89.3%), but it shows every line the gold patch changes on only 39% of the GPT-5.6 issues, against 70% for CQ2-CARE (Appendix Table 15 ). Token compressors lose the verbatim text, and their patches stop applying. The fewer lines a compressor keeps verbatim, the fewer patches apply: from LongCodeZip (96.8% of lines verbatim, 89.7% of patches apply) to LLMLingua-2 (17.5% and 70.7%), against 98.0% for CQ2-CARE. Patches that do not apply account for 28 of the 48 issues that CQ2-CARE resolves and LLMLingua-2 does not; where both patches apply, a smaller gap remains, consistent with altered text also misleading the edit itself. SWE-Pruner, trained to prune lines for coding agents, keeps 91.7% of its lines verbatim and still trails by 2.0 and 7.3 points, because the gaps it leaves inside files cost patches: 93.0% apply with GPT-5.6 and 73.7% with Claude, against 98.0% and 83.3% for CQ2-CARE.

sections.heading: 4.2 Controlled Tests
sections.text: The comparison above is observational: the compressors differ in which files they keep as well as in how they alter them. Two post-hoc tests on all 300 issues change one factor at a time (Figure 2 b; Appendix Table 8 ). Altering the text alone, with the files fixed, costs about ten points. Deleting 20% of the tokens of every line of our own contexts lowers patch applicability from 98.0% to 78.7% and resolution by 9.7 points ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ), while a second patch sample of the intact contexts resolves exactly as many issues. Given the same files, a compressor that cuts whole lines matches CQ2-CARE. This test is a control, not a competing baseline: the compressors cut our own candidate files, built by our localization and evidence step, so they inherit our file choice and only the cut differs. When they cut these files to B i B_{i} instead of the larger single-draw context, LongCodeZip resolves 44.7%, against 43.7% for CQ2-CARE; LLMLingua-2 comes within 3.0 points when its scores choose whole lines, but trails by 7.3 when they choose tokens. CQ2-CARE’s lead over LongCodeZip in the main comparison therefore comes from which files it keeps: cutting the single-draw context lost files to edit that cutting our candidates kept. A within-issue regression over all (issue, context) pairs agrees: verbatim lines and gold-file recall both raise resolution, and the effect of verbatim lines runs mostly through whether the patch applies (Appendix Table 18 b). sections.heading: 4.3 Robustness
sections.text: The baselines still trail ours in four further checks with GPT-5.6 (Table 4 , Figure 3 ; details in Appendix G ). Budget tolerance: the compressors miss the ± \pm 2% window on a quarter to a third of the issues, almost always by landing under budget; on the issues within it, every gap is unchanged or larger. Edit format: with search/replace edits instead of diffs, every baseline still trails ours, and quotes taken from compressed contexts often match no unique location in the real file (on 45 issues for LLMLingua-2, against 4 for CQ2-CARE). Compression rate: at 25%, 50% and 75% of the uncompressed context, no compressor or retriever reaches any exact-file context (Figure 3 ). Patch sampling: a second patch sample moves the rates of CQ2-CARE, LongCodeZip and LLMLingua-2 by at most 2.0 points, and averaged over both samples CQ2-CARE still leads both ( p ≤ 0.002 p\leq 0.002 ).

sections.heading: 4.4 Ablations of CQ2-CARE
sections.text: What makes exact-file selection work is predicting few files, not agreement between samples (Appendix Table 6 ). Agreement raises localization F1 well above a single draw (0.613 vs. 0.430), but only because it names half as many files: a single draw cut to the same number of files reaches 0.600 and resolves about as many issues with both models (Claude: Appendix Table 17 ). More exact files help when the budget allows: the files that either draw names resolve 4.0 points more than CQ2-CARE at 2.3K more tokens, and the agreement thresholds t t -of-5 trade files for tokens smoothly (Figure 3 ). The evidence step adds 3.0 points, short of significance ( p = 0.068 p=0.068 ). Exact-file selection is also the cheaper way to fill the budget. Against the uncompressed single draw, CQ2-CARE uses 0.68 × \times the tokens with GPT-5.6 and passes the planned non-inferiority test; with Claude, it uses 0.73 × \times the tokens and resolves more, but the token ratio’s upper bound narrowly misses its margin (Appendix D ). Its whole pipeline costs $0.151 per issue with GPT-5.6, against $0.199 for the single draw and $0.168–0.177 for the compressor contexts in API calls alone, because those first build the uncompressed context.

sections.heading: Choose files or compress tokens?
sections.text: An agent builder who must cut context can retrieve chunks, prune a larger context, or choose files and show them whole. Retrieval keeps the text but often loses the files to edit, and token pruning keeps the files but alters the text that an edit must quote; each costs on its own (§ 4.2 ). Edits stay locatable only when the text is verbatim (§ 4.3 ), and editing tools that replace a quoted span ( Anthropic, 2024 ; Gauthier, 2026 ) or a numbered line range ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) need exactly this. Choosing files also needs no compression model: LongLLMLingua and LongCodeZip spent a median 34–37 s of GPU time per issue (84–97 s on Claude’s larger contexts, where LongCodeZip ran out of memory on 4 issues at 48 GB), and CQ2-CARE adds one localization call. What the results do not show is that a selector beats a code-aware compressor that starts from the same files: given our candidates, LongCodeZip matched CQ2-CARE, although it still spent 6.8 GPU-hours on 300 issues. We read this as a rule rather than a ranking: choose the candidate files well, then cut whole lines if anything must be cut.

sections.heading: Re-read on demand or compress once?
sections.text: Agents that can re-open files may recover some of the losses we measure, because a compressed view tells them which file to read in full. Each re-read, however, costs a turn and the tokens that compression was meant to save, and a model may not notice that the text it sees is altered: in Figure 1 , it rewrote a line that does not exist in the file. Measuring this trade-off needs a full agent loop, which we leave to future work.

sections.heading: Localization scores or end-to-end tests?
sections.text: Intermediate metrics can mislead. Agreement between two localization samples raises file-level F1 far above a single sample, yet a single sample cut to the same number of files resolves about as many issues (§ 4.4 ). Exit-code grading, which we used before this study, credited an empty patch on 4 of 6 issues (Appendix C ). Context methods for coding agents should therefore be compared end to end, at equal budgets, with the benchmark’s tests.

sections.heading: Prompt compression.
sections.text: Hard prompt compression removes tokens or sentences that a smaller model judges uninformative ( Li et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) ; RECOMP compresses retrieved documents extractively or abstractively ( Xu et al., 2024 ) , and Li et al. (2025) survey the area. On long-context question answering and summarization, Jha et al. (2024) find that extractive, reranker-based selection of chunks often outperforms token pruning and abstractive summarization. We find the same ordering for issue resolution and identify the cost specific to it: edits must quote the text that pruning alters.

sections.heading: Agent memory.
sections.text: Language-agent frameworks separate a working memory, from which each prompt is built, from long-term memories retrieved into it ( Sumers et al., 2024 ) , and MemGPT manages what moves between a limited context and external storage ( Packer et al., 2024 ) ; for a coding agent, the repository is the long-term memory, and the question is which part of it enters the prompt. For code, LongCodeZip keeps whole functions and blocks chosen by perplexity, since its authors note that token-level compression “corrupts code syntax and structure” ( Shi et al., 2025 ) , and perplexity-based pruning removes Python indentation in repository-level completion ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . SWEzze trains a compressor on execution-derived minimal contexts, but compares methods only around fault locations already found by Agentless ( Jia et al., 2026 ) ; SWE-Pruner prunes the lines an agent reads and attributes, as a hypothesis, the losses of LLMLingua-2 and embedding retrieval in a 50-issue comparison to disrupted syntax and missed details ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . SweRank learns to retrieve and rerank whole functions from issue–patch pairs ( Reddy et al., 2026 ) . We instead fix the budget per issue, let each method decide which files enter the context, and measure both failure modes with controlled tests.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We compared ways to fill a coding agent’s context budget at equal per-issue budgets on 300 test-graded issues with two model families. Showing a few whole files verbatim resolved more issues than pruning tokens or retrieving chunks, and about as many as a trained retriever of whole functions, because retrieval often misses the files to edit and token pruning alters the text that patches must quote, and controlled tests showed that each loss costs on its own. For coding agents, the context budget is best spent choosing which code to show, kept verbatim and in whole lines.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: • Setting. We study one patch call per context on Python issues from one benchmark, not a multi-turn agent that could read more files or run tests. • Comparisons. B i B_{i} is our context’s realized size, so we compare at our method’s operating point (the 100-issue rate sweep covers others). File-level BM25, the controlled tests, SWE-Pruner (in its single-turn mode) and SweRank were added after the main results; SweRank may have trained on other pull requests from our repositories, and its small gap to CQ2-CARE does not show equal performance. • Estimator. It uses the gold patch and serves only as a diagnostic; its coverage counted inside functions was chosen after seeing SweRank’s result and needs a test on an unseen method. • Precision and contamination. Most cells have one patch sample, and a second one flips 8.7–18.9% of outcomes, so small gaps such as Claude’s to LLMLingua-2 ( p = 0.027 p=0.027 ) are fragile. The issues may overlap the models’ training data, but the gaps do not shrink detectably on newer issues (Appendix Table 18 a); some may come from repositories seen while developing CQ2-CARE.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: This work evaluates context-compression methods on public open-source repositories and issues. It involves no human subjects or personal data. Generated patches were executed only inside isolated sandboxes. We will release code, prompts and per-issue outcomes.

sections.heading: Appendix B Implementation Details and Compute
sections.text: This appendix gives the details of CQ2-CARE (Algorithm 1 ) and of the baselines. Algorithms 2 – 10 give every other context step in the same notation, with a link to each method’s paper and code, including the two trained methods (Algorithms 6 and 9 ).

sections.heading: Localization and evidence.
sections.text: The path inventory ranks paths by h h , the number of distinct words they share with the issue text and the fixed question the model is asked, with ties broken by h / n h/n , the share of the path’s n n words that match; words are lowercased identifiers and their parts split at punctuation, underscores and case changes, so the example path path/to/file.py in that question makes py a shared word for every Python file. The ranking only decides which paths fit, counting bytes/3 as tokens; the model sees them in alphabetical order, and the list omits files under node_modules , vendor , dist , build , target and .next directories. A salted hash assigns the roles of the five answers drawn per issue: two construction samples L 1 , L 2 L_{1},L_{2} , one comparator L 0 L_{0} , and two that serve only the agreement-threshold sweep. CQ2-CARE keeps the files both construction samples name if they exist in the repository, even if they were cut from the inventory, drops paths under test(s) / doc(s) directories and orders the rest by summed reciprocal rank; it falls back on L 0 L_{0} when a sample is malformed or nothing remains (1.7% of issues with GPT-5.6, 0.3% with Claude). Each evidence search (e.g., a definition, callers, a literal string, related tests) becomes up to eight fixed strings for git grep at the base commit and adds a span from each of at most two new files, eight in total: the enclosing Python definition of the match or a window of lines around it. A selected file over 60K tokens is cut to its first 60K, selected non-code files are not shown (13 files), evidence spans are capped at 12K tokens each, and any block that would take the context past 80K tokens is skipped; with GPT-5.6, 7 of 300 contexts reach a cap.

sections.heading: Models and calls.
sections.text: Every call uses the same model per run: gpt-5.6-sol through the Azure OpenAI Responses API, or Claude Opus 5 through Microsoft Foundry, with medium reasoning effort and the providers’ default sampling. Output limits are 6,144 tokens for localization, 4,096 for the planner and 32,768 for patches. Requests are byte-identical across contexts except for the context; failed transport calls are retried, and refusals or truncated answers count as unresolved. Localization returns a ranked JSON list of paths; the planner returns at most four typed search requests; the patch call returns a unified diff (or, in the edit-format control, search/replace edits, located by exact and then whitespace-tolerant matching) in a JSON field. Post-processing, identical for every context, fixes diff headers and hunk line counts and re-anchors a hunk only when its original lines match the base-commit source exactly and uniquely; it never reads tests or the gold patch.

sections.heading: Contexts.
sections.text: Token counts use the o200k tokenizer. Repository names, instance identifiers and commit hashes are masked in everything the model sees. Compressors search only their own rate setting for the closest result within ± \pm 2% of B i B_{i} (at most 16 settings per issue) and keep span headers verbatim. LLMLingua-2 uses the xlm-roberta-large MeetingBank classifier and keeps the highest-scored words within each chunk of up to 512 tokens; LongLLMLingua takes the issue as the question, drops and reorders whole spans, then prunes tokens at a rate set per span; LongCodeZip, with the settings of its paper, keeps the top-ranked functions and chooses blocks within them by a knapsack. Chunk BM25 uses k 1 = 1.2 k_{1}{=}1.2 , b = 0.75 b{=}0.75 ; chunk BM25 and dense retrieval rank top-level Python definitions and the code between them, or 60-line windows for other files and for definitions over 4K tokens, and cut the first unit that does not fit to its longest whole-line prefix before stopping; CodeRankEmbed uses cosine similarity, batch size 8 and a 4,096-token limit. File-level BM25 reproduces SWE-bench’s make_datasets procedure ( swebench 4.0.3): every Python file whose path does not contain the word test , tests or testing is one document (its path followed by its contents), BM25 uses Pyserini’s default k 1 = 0.9 k_{1}{=}0.9 , b = 0.4 b{=}0.4 with our code tokenizer, and the top 20 files are added whole in rank order, skipping any file that does not fit in B i B_{i} . LongLLMLingua and LongCodeZip ran on RTX A6000 GPUs, LLMLingua-2 on CPU.

sections.heading: Grading and statistics.
sections.text: The SWE-rebench fork of the SWE-bench harness ( swebench 4.0.3) runs in Apptainer sandboxes built from the benchmark’s images, with a fresh overlay per context and a 30-minute limit per evaluation. Of the 340 drawn candidates, 10 gold patches failed and 2 empty patches passed the eligibility check. Bootstrap intervals use 20,000 issue resamples with seed 20260927; McNemar tests are exact; missing outcomes count as unresolved.

sections.heading: Hardware and cost.
sections.text: Grading ran on CPU cores of a shared GPU cluster; LongLLMLingua, LongCodeZip and dense retrieval ran on RTX A6000 (48 GB) and A100 (40 GB) GPUs, and LLMLingua-2 on CPU. For the GPT-5.6 study they used 6.5, 8.3 and 3.3 GPU-hours, and LLMLingua-2 1.3 CPU-hours; for Claude’s larger contexts, LongLLMLingua and LongCodeZip used 14.2 and 11.4 GPU-hours. LongCodeZip on our candidate files used 6.8 GPU-hours. API cost at 2026 list prices was about $830 for GPT-5.6 (including $43 for the 100-issue controlled tests, $179 for the 300-issue controlled tests and the second patch sample, $23 for the search/replace runs of three more baselines and $27 for file-level BM25) and $1,438 for Claude Opus 5, including $35 for its gold-file oracle on the 200 issues the first run had not covered, $93 for file-level BM25 and about $170 of duplicate patch calls from a pipeline error, which we graded as a second patch sample. sections.heading: Grading with exit codes is not grading resolution.
sections.text: Before this study, our resolution numbers came from an executor that marked an issue resolved when the repository’s test command exited with code 0, without applying the issue’s test patch or checking the FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS lists. On 6 issues we checked, an empty patch counted as resolved on 4 under that rule and on 0 under official grading. That rule largely measures whether the existing test suite passes. All results in this paper use official grading, and every issue was checked in advance to be resolved by its gold patch and not by an empty patch.

sections.heading: Budget matching is fiddly.
sections.text: Rate knobs are coarse (LLMLingua-2 quantizes its threshold to 1%; LongCodeZip’s rate cannot be set to 1.0 because of an upstream bug), so we search a fixed grid with interpolation and record misses rather than re-running with other settings. Span headers count toward the budget and are kept verbatim for every method, so compressors never lose file identity.

sections.heading: Infrastructure.
sections.text: Model-based compressors ran out of memory on the largest contexts; we released GPU memory between issues and retried those issues in a fresh process with expandable memory segments, and LongCodeZip still failed on 4 of Claude’s 300 contexts, even on a 48 GB A6000 (counted as unresolved; in the worst case for CQ2-CARE the LongCodeZip contrast keeps p = 0.003 p=0.003 ). With Claude, one issue’s tests hung in two separate grading runs for every context, although they had passed in the eligibility check; it is counted as unresolved for all contexts, which leaves every paired contrast unchanged. Parallel container builds into a cold shared cache corrupted it, so builds are serialized.

Heavy deletion has a different failure with Claude: 36 of its 300 answers on LongLLMLingua contexts failed to parse, 31 of them placeholders or empty patches such as "..." , "<unified diff>" or "d i ff . . ." that echo the compressed text; 35 of these 36 issues received well-formed patches on LLMLingua-2 contexts. Claude’s localization keeps more files, so its contexts are about twice as large as GPT’s (27.1K vs. 13.8K mean tokens for CQ2-CARE). Against the uncompressed single draw, CQ2-CARE resolves more (46.7% vs. 43.0%) at 0.73 × \times the tokens, but the token ratio’s upper bound (0.757) just misses H4’s 0.75 margin. With Claude, the gold-file oracle resolves 46.3%, about as often as CQ2-CARE (46.7%); its patches apply on 83.0% of issues. sections.text: The compressors miss the ± \pm 2% window on 26.3–34.3% of issues; within it, LongCodeZip trails by 6.6 points on 197 issues (Holm p = 0.010 p=0.010 ) and LLMLingua-2 by 16.7 on 221. In the rate sweep, LongCodeZip reaches at most 37.0% (at 12.6K tokens), LLMLingua-2 32.0% and chunk BM25 25.0% (at about 13K), while exact-file contexts resolve 41.0–44.0% between 11.9K and 15.1K tokens. sections.heading: The frozen predictions.
sections.text: We built the contexts of SWE-Pruner and SweRank, computed the four predictions and froze them (file hash and time stamp in the repository) before generating any of their patches. The estimator predicts both SWE-Pruner rates inside their intervals and underpredicts SweRank by 5.3 and 7.5 points (Table 13 ). The misses are concentrated where SweRank shows the whole function to edit but leaves out changed lines outside functions, such as imports, module constants and class attributes. Counting κ \kappa over the changed lines inside functions only, without refitting, moves both SweRank predictions to within their intervals and leaves the fit to the main study and its accuracy on the left-out contexts unchanged. This correction was chosen after the outcomes, so it must be tested on a method the estimator has not seen.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.21073v1 [cs.SE] 15 Oct 2026 Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files Xiaocong Yang * Rishit Chatterjee * Himanshu Udupi Affiliation: Vikram Ramavarapu ChengXiang Zhai Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Affiliation: {xy51, rc33, hudupi2, vikramr2, czhai}@illinois.edu Abstract A coding agent works on repositories that can be far larger than its context window can hold. Prompt compressors and retrievers offer solutions to this problem, but patching an issue needs two things at once: the files that must change, and their code exactly as written, since the model must reproduce the lines it edits. Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget. We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks. We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark’s tests. With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3). Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits. * * footnotetext: Equal contribution. 1 Introduction Agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) now resolve real software issues end to end: they read an issue, explore a repository and write a patch that the project’s tests accept ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2025 ) . Managing what enters their context already makes them cheaper: it can halve an agent’s cost ( Lindenbauer et al., 2025 ) or cut it by a fifth to a third ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) . Every prompt token is paid for on every call, and models use information in the middle of a long input less reliably than at its ends ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Figure 1: An issue sample under different compression methods. The issue ( pypa__twine-1225 ) reports error messages that lack the f of an f-string; the gold patch edits twine/sdist.py . ρ \rho : gold-file recall, the share of the gold-patch files in the context m m ; ε \varepsilon : the share of m m ’s lines that are verbatim. BM25 fills B i B_{i} with issue templates (two of three spans shown), so its patch guesses lines it never saw; LLMLingua-2 deletes tokens (struck out), among them the f of line 23, so its patch rewrites a line that does not exist; ours shows the file verbatim. Indentation is trimmed; an ellipsis marks an elided prefix. Chosen for illustration as the smallest of the 4 such issues out of 300 (a random one is in Appendix A ). Right: resolution with GPT-5.6 (solid) and Claude Opus 5 (light), every context fitted to B i B_{i} . SWE-Pruner, a line pruner trained for coding agents, is the last bar of the pruning group, and SweRank, a trained retriever of whole functions, the last bar of the retrieval group. Yet every step still needs code in the prompt, and a coding agent’s context window is small next to the repositories it works on: SWE-bench codebases average 3,010 non-test files and 438K lines ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) . We therefore treat the repository as the agent’s memory and the prompt as a compressed view of it, one that leaves most of the code out. To resolve an issue, the view still has to keep two things: the files the fix must edit, and their text exactly as it is. For anyone building a coding agent, this raises a practical question: at a fixed token budget, which compression of the repository lets the model resolve the most issues? Three lines of work each study part of this question: prompt compression for long natural-language prompts ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) , retrieval of repository code for code completion and issue resolution ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , and issue-resolution systems that prune what an agent reads ( Wang et al., 2026 ) or compress the context around known fault locations ( Jia et al., 2026 ) . Figure 1 shows how the first two can fail on one issue from our study, a report that some error messages lack the f of an f-string. A chunk retriever fills the budget with the repository’s issue templates, which share the report’s wording, and never shows the file to edit. A token pruner keeps that file but deletes f prefixes and quotation marks, so the model’s patch rewrites a line that does not exist and fails to apply. Shown the file whole and verbatim, the same model writes the fix. None of these lines of work compares retrieval, token pruning and file selection at a matched budget per issue, with each method free to decide which files enter the context. Both failures follow from how these tools work. Retrievers rank chunks or files by their similarity to the issue ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ; Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Suresh et al., 2025 ) , so text that echoes the report can outrank the file to edit. Prompt compressors delete the tokens or code blocks that a small model scores as least useful ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) ; this costs little when the output is an answer or a summary, but an edit must quote the code it changes exactly ( Xia et al., 2025 ; Anthropic, 2024 ; Gauthier, 2026 ) . The remedy follows: spend the budget on choosing which files to show, and show them whole and verbatim, so that edits quote text that exists and no compression model runs in the loop. Since each chosen file is shown whole, the selector must name few files, and the right ones. We therefore build a simple selector, CQ2-CARE, that asks the model under test twice, independently, which files must change and keeps the files both answers name, taking agreement between samples as a sign of reliability ( Wang et al., 2023 ) ; it then adds the short spans that grep finds for definitions, callers or strings the model requests, so code the fix depends on is shown verbatim even outside the chosen files. Its strength is its choice of unit, not its sampling scheme: a single answer cut to the same number of files does about as well, so what matters is choosing few files well (§ 4.4 ). We test this remedy in a controlled comparison on 300 issues from the SWE-rebench leaderboard ( Badertdinov et al., 2025 ) , one per repository: a fixed model receives the issue and one context fitted to the size of the CQ2-CARE context for that issue, writes one patch, and the benchmark’s harness grades it with the issue’s tests. We describe each context by its gold-file recall, the share of the files to edit that it contains, and by the share of its lines that are verbatim, and we run controlled tests that change one of the two at a time. With each of two model families, the selector resolves more issues than each of three compressors and three retrievers, among them SWE-bench’s file-level BM25; with Claude, its lead over one compressor, LLMLingua-2, is narrow. The losses separate cleanly: retrievers keep the text verbatim but often miss the files to edit, and token pruners keep those files but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Controlled tests show that each loss costs on its own: deleting tokens from the selector’s own contexts, with the files unchanged, costs about as much as the compressors lose in the main comparison, while a compressor that keeps whole lines matches the selector when it starts from the same files. The selector even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution: SWE-Pruner, a line pruner, and SweRank, a retriever that shows whole functions verbatim and comes within two points. Our contributions are as follows: • CQ2-CARE, a simple selector that spends the context budget on the files the model names and shows them verbatim, with no compression model (§ 2 ). • A budget-matched, test-graded comparison of CQ2-CARE with three prompt compressors, three retrievers, among them SWE-bench’s file-level BM25, and two methods trained for issue resolution, on 300 issues and two model families (§ 3.3 ). • A decomposition of the losses into gold-file recall and verbatim lines, with controlled tests that change one at a time (§ 4.1 – 4.2 ). 2 Context as Compressed Memory Let R R be the repository at the issue’s base commit (the agent’s memory), q q the issue text and B B a token budget. An agent builder who must cut context can retrieve chunks, prune a larger context, or choose files and show them whole. Retrieval keeps the text but often loses the files to edit, and token pruning keeps the files but alters the text that an edit must quote; each costs on its own (§ 4.2 ). Edits stay locatable only when the text is verbatim (§ 4.3 ), and editing tools that replace a quoted span ( Anthropic, 2024 ; Gauthier, 2026 ) or a numbered line range ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) need exactly this. Choosing files also needs no compression model: LongLLMLingua and LongCodeZip spent a median 34–37 s of GPU time per issue (84–97 s on Claude’s larger contexts, where LongCodeZip ran out of memory on 4 issues at 48 GB), and CQ2-CARE adds one localization call. What the results do not show is that a selector beats a code-aware compressor that starts from the same files: given our candidates, LongCodeZip matched CQ2-CARE, although it still spent 6.8 GPU-hours on 300 issues. We read this as a rule rather than a ranking: choose the candidate files well, then cut whole lines if anything must be cut. Re-read on demand or compress once? Agents that can re-open files may recover some of the losses we measure, because a compressed view tells them which file to read in full. Each re-read, however, costs a turn and the tokens that compression was meant to save, and a model may not notice that the text it sees is altered: in Figure 1 , it rewrote a line that does not exist in the file. Measuring this trade-off needs a full agent loop, which we leave to future work. Localization scores or end-to-end tests? Intermediate metrics can mislead. Agreement between two localization samples raises file-level F1 far above a single sample, yet a single sample cut to the same number of files resolves about as many issues (§ 4.4 ). Exit-code grading, which we used before this study, credited an empty patch on 4 of 6 issues (Appendix C ). Context methods for coding agents should therefore be compared end to end, at equal budgets, with the benchmark’s tests. 6 Related Work Prompt compression. Hard prompt compression removes tokens or sentences that a smaller model judges uninformative ( Li et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) ; RECOMP compresses retrieved documents extractively or abstractively ( Xu et al., 2024 ) , and Li et al. (2025) survey the area. On long-context question answering and summarization, Jha et al. (2024) find that extractive, reranker-based selection of chunks often outperforms token pruning and abstractive summarization. We find the same ordering for issue resolution and identify the cost specific to it: edits must quote the text that pruning alters. Agent memory. Language-agent frameworks separate a working memory, from which each prompt is built, from long-term memories retrieved into it ( Sumers et al., 2024 ) , and MemGPT manages what moves between a limited context and external storage ( Packer et al., 2024 ) ; for a coding agent, the repository is the long-term memory, and the question is which part of it enters the prompt. For code, LongCodeZip keeps whole functions and blocks chosen by perplexity, since its authors note that token-level compression “corrupts code syntax and structure” ( Shi et al., 2025 ) , and perplexity-based pruning removes Python indentation in repository-level completion ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . SWEzze trains a compressor on execution-derived minimal contexts, but compares methods only around fault locations already found by Agentless ( Jia et al., 2026 ) ; SWE-Pruner prunes the lines an agent reads and attributes, as a hypothesis, the losses of LLMLingua-2 and embedding retrieval in a 50-issue comparison to disrupted syntax and missed details ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . SweRank learns to retrieve and rerank whole functions from issue–patch pairs ( Reddy et al., 2026 ) . We instead fix the budget per issue, let each method decide which files enter the context, and measure both failure modes with controlled tests. 7 Conclusion We compared ways to fill a coding agent’s context budget at equal per-issue budgets on 300 test-graded issues with two model families. Showing a few whole files verbatim resolved more issues than pruning tokens or retrieving chunks, and about as many as a trained retriever of whole functions, because retrieval often misses the files to edit and token pruning alters the text that patches must quote, and controlled tests showed that each loss costs on its own. For coding agents, the context budget is best spent choosing which code to show, kept verbatim and in whole lines. Limitations • Setting. We study one patch call per context on Python issues from one benchmark, not a multi-turn agent that could read more files or run tests. • Comparisons. B i B_{i} is our context’s realized size, so we compare at our method’s operating point (the 100-issue rate sweep covers others). File-level BM25, the controlled tests, SWE-Pruner (in its single-turn mode) and SweRank were added after the main results; SweRank may have trained on other pull requests from our repositories, and its small gap to CQ2-CARE does not show equal performance. • Estimator. It uses the gold patch and serves only as a diagnostic; its coverage counted inside functions was chosen after seeing SweRank’s result and needs a test on an unseen method. • Precision and contamination. Most cells have one patch sample, and a second one flips 8.7–18.9% of outcomes, so small gaps such as Claude’s to LLMLingua-2 ( p = 0.027 p=0.027 ) are fragile. The issues may overlap the models’ training data, but the gaps do not shrink detectably on newer issues (Appendix Table 18 a); some may come from repositories seen while developing CQ2-CARE. The path inventory ranks paths by h h , the number of distinct words they share with the issue text and the fixed question the model is asked, with ties broken by h / n h/n , the share of the path’s n n words that match; words are lowercased identifiers and their parts split at punctuation, underscores and case changes, so the example path path/to/file.py in that question makes py a shared word for every Python file. The ranking only decides which paths fit, counting bytes/3 as tokens; the model sees them in alphabetical order, and the list omits files under node_modules , vendor , dist , build , target and .next directories. A salted hash assigns the roles of the five answers drawn per issue: two construction samples L 1 , L 2 L_{1},L_{2} , one comparator L 0 L_{0} , and two that serve only the agreement-threshold sweep. CQ2-CARE keeps the files both construction samples name if they exist in the repository, even if they were cut from the inventory, drops paths under test(s) / doc(s) directories and orders the rest by summed reciprocal rank; it falls back on L 0 L_{0} when a sample is malformed or nothing remains (1.7% of issues with GPT-5.6, 0.3% with Claude). Each evidence search (e.g., a definition, callers, a literal string, related tests) becomes up to eight fixed strings for git grep at the base commit and adds a span from each of at most two new files, eight in total: the enclosing Python definition of the match or a window of lines around it. A selected file over 60K tokens is cut to its first 60K, selected non-code files are not shown (13 files), evidence spans are capped at 12K tokens each, and any block that would take the context past 80K tokens is skipped; with GPT-5.6, 7 of 300 contexts reach a cap. Models and calls. Every call uses the same model per run: gpt-5.6-sol through the Azure OpenAI Responses API, or Claude Opus 5 through Microsoft Foundry, with medium reasoning effort and the providers’ default sampling. Output limits are 6,144 tokens for localization, 4,096 for the planner and 32,768 for patches. Requests are byte-identical across contexts except for the context; failed transport calls are retried, and refusals or truncated answers count as unresolved. Localization returns a ranked JSON list of paths; the planner returns at most four typed search requests; the patch call returns a unified diff (or, in the edit-format control, search/replace edits, located by exact and then whitespace-tolerant matching) in a JSON field. Post-processing, identical for every context, fixes diff headers and hunk line counts and re-anchors a hunk only when its original lines match the base-commit source exactly and uniquely; it never reads tests or the gold patch. Contexts. Token counts use the o200k tokenizer. Repository names, instance identifiers and commit hashes are masked in everything the model sees. Compressors search only their own rate setting for the closest result within ± \pm 2% of B i B_{i} (at most 16 settings per issue) and keep span headers verbatim. LLMLingua-2 uses the xlm-roberta-large MeetingBank classifier and keeps the highest-scored words within each chunk of up to 512 tokens; LongLLMLingua takes the issue as the question, drops and reorders whole spans, then prunes tokens at a rate set per span; LongCodeZip, with the settings of its paper, keeps the top-ranked functions and chooses blocks within them by a knapsack. Chunk BM25 uses k 1 = 1.2 k_{1}{=}1.2 , b = 0.75 b{=}0.75 ; chunk BM25 and dense retrieval rank top-level Python definitions and the code between them, or 60-line windows for other files and for definitions over 4K tokens, and cut the first unit that does not fit to its longest whole-line prefix before stopping; CodeRankEmbed uses cosine similarity, batch size 8 and a 4,096-token limit. File-level BM25 reproduces SWE-bench’s make_datasets procedure ( swebench 4.0.3): every Python file whose path does not contain the word test , tests or testing is one document (its path followed by its contents), BM25 uses Pyserini’s default k 1 = 0.9 k_{1}{=}0.9 , b = 0.4 b{=}0.4 with our code tokenizer, and the top 20 files are added whole in rank order, skipping any file that does not fit in B i B_{i} . LongLLMLingua and LongCodeZip ran on RTX A6000 GPUs, LLMLingua-2 on CPU. Grading and statistics. The SWE-rebench fork of the SWE-bench harness ( swebench 4.0.3) runs in Apptainer sandboxes built from the benchmark’s images, with a fresh overlay per context and a 30-minute limit per evaluation. Of the 340 drawn candidates, 10 gold patches failed and 2 empty patches passed the eligibility check. Bootstrap intervals use 20,000 issue resamples with seed 20260927; McNemar tests are exact; missing outcomes count as unresolved. Hardware and cost. Grading ran on CPU cores of a shared GPU cluster; LongLLMLingua, LongCodeZip and dense retrieval ran on RTX A6000 (48 GB) and A100 (40 GB) GPUs, and LLMLingua-2 on CPU. For the GPT-5.6 study they used 6.5, 8.3 and 3.3 GPU-hours, and LLMLingua-2 1.3 CPU-hours; for Claude’s larger contexts, LongLLMLingua and LongCodeZip used 14.2 and 11.4 GPU-hours. LongCodeZip on our candidate files used 6.8 GPU-hours. Before this study, our resolution numbers came from an executor that marked an issue resolved when the repository’s test command exited with code 0, without applying the issue’s test patch or checking the FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS lists. On 6 issues we checked, an empty patch counted as resolved on 4 under that rule and on 0 under official grading. That rule largely measures whether the existing test suite passes. All results in this paper use official grading, and every issue was checked in advance to be resolved by its gold patch and not by an empty patch. Budget matching is fiddly. Rate knobs are coarse (LLMLingua-2 quantizes its threshold to 1%; LongCodeZip’s rate cannot be set to 1.0 because of an upstream bug), so we search a fixed grid with interpolation and record misses rather than re-running with other settings. Span headers count toward the budget and are kept verbatim for every method, so compressors never lose file identity. Infrastructure. Model-based compressors ran out of memory on the largest contexts; we released GPU memory between issues and retried those issues in a fresh process with expandable memory segments, and LongCodeZip still failed on 4 of Claude’s 300 contexts, even on a 48 GB A6000 (counted as unresolved; in the worst case for CQ2-CARE the LongCodeZip contrast keeps p = 0.003 p=0.003 ). With Claude, one issue’s tests hung in two separate grading runs for every context, although they had passed in the eligibility check; it is counted as unresolved for all contexts, which leaves every paired contrast unchanged. Parallel container builds into a cold shared cache corrupted it, so builds are serialized.
